paragraphs: Father Païssy was right, of course, to decide that his “dear boy” would come back. He may even have seen, to some degree, what Alyosha’s spiritual state really meant. Still, I have to admit that I would find it very hard to give a clear account of that strange, hazy time in the life of the young hero I love so much. Father Païssy asked sadly, “Are you too with those of little faith?” I could answer confidently for Alyosha, “No, he is not with those of little faith. Quite the opposite.” All his trouble, in fact, came from having great faith. But the trouble was there just the same, and it hurt so badly that even long afterwards Alyosha remembered that sorrowful day as one of the bitterest and most fatal of his life. Suppose someone asks: “Can all his grief and turmoil really have come only from the fact that his elder’s body showed signs of early decay, instead of working miracles at once?” I have to answer without beating about the bush, “Yes, it certainly can.” I only ask the reader not to hurry to laugh at my young hero’s pure heart. I have no wish to apologize for him, or to excuse his innocent faith by pointing to his youth, or how little he had studied, or any such thing. On the contrary, I declare that I truly respect the qualities of his heart. A youth who took in impressions cautiously, whose love was lukewarm, and whose mind was too prudent for his age and therefore worth little, might well, I admit, have escaped what happened to my hero. But sometimes it does a man more credit to be swept away by a feeling, however unreasonable, that grows out of great love, than to remain unmoved. This is even truer in youth, because a young man who is always sensible is not to be trusted and is worth little—that’s my opinion!
“But,” reasonable people will perhaps cry, “not every young man can believe in such a superstition, and your hero is no example for others.”
To this I answer once more, “Yes! My hero had faith, a holy and steadfast faith, but I am still not going to apologize for him.”

Earlier I declared, perhaps too hastily, that I would not explain or justify my hero. Now I see that some explanation is needed if the rest of my story is to make sense. So let me say it plainly: miracles were not the issue. He had no frivolous, impatient expectation of miracles. Nor did Alyosha need miracles just then to prove some idea he had already formed—oh, no, not at all. Before everything else he saw one figure—the figure of his beloved elder, the holy man he revered with such adoration. All the love hidden in his pure young heart for everyone and everything had, for the past year, been gathered up—wrongly, perhaps—and fixed on one person, his beloved elder. It is true that he had held this person for so long as his ideal that all his young strength and energy could only turn toward it, until for the moment he forgot “everyone and everything.” Later he remembered that on that terrible day he had entirely forgotten his brother Dmitri, whom he had worried over so anxiously the day before. He had also forgotten to take the two hundred roubles to Ilusha’s father, though he had meant so warmly to do it the evening before. But again, what he needed was not miracles, only “the higher justice,” which in his belief had been outraged by the blow that had so suddenly and cruelly wounded his heart. And what does it matter that this “justice” he looked for naturally took the form of miracles, to be worked at once by the ashes of his adored teacher? Everyone in the monastery cherished the same thought and the same hope, even those whose minds Alyosha respected, Father Païssy himself, for instance. So Alyosha, with no doubts to disturb him, dressed his dreams in the same form as everyone else. And a whole year in the monastery had made this expectation a habit of his heart. But it was justice, justice, that he thirsted for, not simply miracles.

And now the man who, in his belief, should have been lifted above everyone in the whole world, instead of receiving the glory due to him, was suddenly disgraced and dishonored! What for? Who had judged him? Who could have decreed this? These were the questions that tore at his inexperienced, untouched heart. He could not bear it without mortification, even resentment, that the holiest of holy men should be held up to the jeers and spiteful mockery of a frivolous crowd so far beneath him. Suppose there had been no miracles, suppose nothing marvelous had come to justify his hopes: why this insult, why this humiliation, why this early decay, “in excess of nature,” as the spiteful monks put it? Why this “sign from heaven,” which they greeted so triumphantly together with Father Ferapont, and why did they think they had won the right to greet it? Where is the finger of Providence? Why did Providence hide its face “at the most critical moment” (so Alyosha thought it), as though it chose to bow to the blind, dumb, pitiless laws of nature?

That was why Alyosha’s heart was bleeding. And of course, as I have said already, the sting of it all was that the man he loved above everything on earth had been put to shame and humiliated! This murmuring may have been shallow and unreasonable in my hero. But I say for the third time—and I am ready to admit that my feeling may be hard to defend—that I am glad he showed himself not too reasonable at that moment. A sensible man always comes back to reason in time. But if love does not win in a boy’s heart at such an exceptional moment, when will it? I will not, however, skip over something strange that rose for a while to the surface of Alyosha’s mind in this fatal, confused moment. This new something was the harassing impression left by the conversation with Ivan, which kept coming back to haunt him. At this moment it haunted him. Oh, it was not that something of the fundamental, elemental, so to speak, faith of his soul had been shaken. He loved his God and believed in Him steadfastly, though he was suddenly murmuring against Him. But a vague, tormenting, evil impression from his conversation with Ivan the day before had suddenly come back to life in his soul, and it seemed to be pushing its way up into his consciousness.

Dusk was falling when Rakitin, who was crossing the pine copse from the hermitage to the monastery, suddenly noticed Alyosha. He lay face down on the ground under a tree, motionless, apparently asleep. Rakitin went over and called his name.
“You here, Alexey? Can it be—” he began in surprise, but stopped. He had meant to say, “Can it be that you’ve come to this?”
Alyosha did not look at him, but a slight movement told Rakitin at once that he had heard and understood.
“What’s the matter?” he went on; but the surprise on his face slowly turned into a smile that grew more and more ironical.
“Listen, I’ve been hunting for you for the past two hours. You just vanished. What are you doing? What sort of foolery is this? You could at least look at me...”
Alyosha lifted his head, sat up and leaned his back against the tree. He was not crying, but his face showed pain and irritation. He did not look at Rakitin, though; he looked away, past him.
“Do you know, your face has completely changed? Not a trace of your famous mildness left. Are you angry with someone? Has someone been treating you badly?”
“Leave me alone,” said Alyosha suddenly, with a weary wave of his hand, still looking away.

“Oho! So that’s how we’re feeling! So you can snap at people like the rest of us mortals. That’s quite a come-down from the angels. Listen, Alyosha, you’ve surprised me, do you hear? I mean it. It’s been a long time since anything here surprised me. I always took you for an educated man....”
Alyosha finally looked at him, but in a vague way, as if he barely understood what Rakitin was saying.
“Are you really this upset just because your old man has started to stink? Surely you didn’t seriously believe he was going to work miracles?” exclaimed Rakitin, truly astonished again.
“I believed, I believe, I want to believe, and I will believe—what more do you want?” cried Alyosha irritably.

“Nothing at all, my boy. Damn it all! No schoolboy of thirteen believes in that now. But there.... So now you’re in a temper with your God, you’re rebelling against Him; He hasn’t promoted you, He hasn’t handed you the medal of merit! Eh, what a bunch you are!”
Alyosha gazed at Rakitin for a long while with his eyes half shut, and suddenly a gleam came into them ... but it was not anger at Rakitin.
“I am not rebelling against my God; I simply ‘don’t accept His world.’” Alyosha suddenly gave a forced smile.
“What do you mean, you don’t accept the world?” Rakitin thought a moment over his answer. “What kind of idiocy is that?”
Alyosha did not answer.
“Come on, enough of this nonsense, now to business. Have you had anything to eat today?”
“I don’t remember.... I think I have.”

“You need building up, judging by your face. It’s painful to look at you. You didn’t sleep all night either, I hear; you had a meeting in there. And then all this uproar afterwards. Most likely you’ve had nothing but a mouthful of holy bread. I’ve got a sausage in my pocket; I brought it from town in case of need, only you won’t eat sausage....”
“Give me some.”

“Well, well! You’re really going at it! Why, it’s a full mutiny, with barricades! Right, my boy, we must make the most of this. Come to my place.... I wouldn’t mind a drop of vodka myself, I’m dead tired. Vodka would be going too far for you, I suppose ... or would you like some?”
“Give me vodka too.”
“Well, well! You surprise me, brother!” Rakitin stared at him in amazement. “Anyway, vodka or sausage, this is a damned fine chance and we mustn’t miss it. Come on.”
Alyosha got up without a word and followed Rakitin.
“If your little brother Ivan could see this—wouldn’t he be surprised! By the way, your brother Ivan left for Moscow this morning, did you know?”

“Yes,” answered Alyosha listlessly. Suddenly the image of his brother Dmitri rose in his mind. But it stayed only a minute. It reminded him of something that could not be put off for a moment, some duty, some terrible obligation. Yet even that reminder made no impression on him. It did not reach his heart, and it faded from his mind at once and was forgotten. But, a long while afterwards, Alyosha remembered this.

“Your brother Ivan once declared that I was a ‘liberal booby with no talents whatsoever.’ And you, once, couldn’t help letting me know I was ‘dishonorable.’ Well! Now I’d like to see what your talents and your sense of honor do for you.” Rakitin finished this speech to himself in a whisper.

“Listen!” he said aloud, “let’s take the path beyond the monastery, straight into town. Hm! I should stop at Madame Hohlakov’s on the way. Just imagine, I wrote and told her everything that happened, and would you believe it, she answered me right away in pencil (the lady is mad about writing notes) that ‘she would never have expected _such conduct_ from a man of such a reverend character as Father Zossima.’ That was her very word: ‘conduct.’ She’s angry too. Eh, what a bunch you are! Wait!” he cried suddenly. He stopped short and, taking Alyosha by the shoulder, made him stop as well.

“Do you know, Alyosha,” he peered into his eyes with curiosity. A new thought had suddenly come to him. He was laughing on the surface, but he was clearly afraid to say it aloud, because he still found it so hard to believe in the strange, unexpected mood he now saw in Alyosha. “Alyosha, do you know where we’d better go?” he finally brought out, timidly and insinuatingly.
“I don’t care ... wherever you like.”
“Let’s go to Grushenka, eh? Will you come?” Rakitin said at last, trembling with timid suspense.
“Let’s go to Grushenka,” Alyosha answered calmly, at once, and this quick, calm agreement startled Rakitin so much that he nearly jumped back.
“Well! Would you listen to that!” he cried in amazement, but he took firm hold of Alyosha’s arm and led him down the path, still afraid that he would change his mind.
They walked on in silence; Rakitin was honestly afraid to speak.

“And how glad she’ll be, how delighted!” he muttered, but fell silent again. And in fact it was not to please Grushenka that he was taking Alyosha to her. He was a practical man and never undertook anything unless he saw some gain for himself. Here his purpose was twofold. First came a vengeful wish to see “the downfall of the righteous,” Alyosha’s fall “from the saints to the sinners,” which he was already gloating over in his imagination. Second, he had in view a certain material gain for himself, which will be explained later.
“So the critical moment has come,” he thought to himself with spiteful glee, “and we’ll catch it on the hop, because it’s exactly what we want.”
